newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG mercenaries ask about evacuation to Australia.
newsitem.headline: PNG mercenaries ask about evacuation to Australia.

text.p: Mercenaries training Papua New Guinea troops for a strike against rebels on Bougainville have asked two Australian hospitals about emergency medical treatment for casualties, hospital officals said.
News of the inquiries came as Papua New Guinea on Thursday said the mercenaries would not be used in any frontline attack on rebels, but act only as advisers.

The mercenaries are currently training a small group of Papua New Guinea soldiers with the aim of launching an attack to end the nine-year conflict on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of the Papua New Guinea capital Port Moresby.

The Cairns and Townsville hospitals in northern Queensland state said they had received letters last Friday from the London-based Sandline International, the mercenary company hired by Papua New Guinea.
The letters titled "Casualty Evacuation From Papua New Guinea" inquired about emergency medical facilities and the evacuation of casualties from Papua New Guinea to Australia.
"...I am constructing the medical scheme for our employers," a Sandline representative in Port Moresby said in the letters, released by the Queensland state health minister.
"Part of this medical scheme will entail an evacuation plan to neighbouring Australia in the event where a critically ill patient cannot receive further medical attention in PNG."
The letters also asked for 24-hour emergency hospital contacts and the cost involved.
Both hospitals have told the mercenaries they would take injured soldiers on "humanitarian grounds", but the Queensland government has told Papua New Guinea that it would be billed.

Papua New Guinea has hired 40 mercenaries from Sandline International, a subsidiary of British-registered Executive Outcomes, Africa's best known private army and which has helped Angola and Sierra Leone fight rebel threats.
Papua New Guinea on Thursday said it would not break its contract with the mercenaries, despite diplomatic pressure from Australia, New Zealand and Britain.
Papua New Guinea Defence Force Minister Mathias Ijape said his government was forced to use mercenaries to boost defence capabilities because Australia had refused to do the job.

"We have requested the Australians help us build our capabilities, but...they have always said they will not help us in our capability building, but they will help us in our training," Ijape told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"That sort of left us in a limbo. We had to look elsewhere."
Australia on Wednesday stepped up its diplomatic campaign against the mercenaries, summoning Port Moresby's top diplomat for a detailed explanation.
Papua New Guinea has said the mercenaries would not be used to fight rebels, but would act only as military advisers.
Ijape said of Sandline's letters to Australian hospitals: "In the course of their advisory engagement they could be hurt. They are probably getting themselves prepared for that."
The British High Commission in Port Moresby on Thursday issued a statement criticising the use of mercenaries.
"Britain believes the use of private military consultants will only prolong the Bougainville conflict," it said.
